title: How did Gutenberg cast his type?
short: Glyph-level variation in the earliest Mainz types has been read both as evidence against the punch, matrix and hand mould, and as fully compatible with it.
matters: The standard account of printing's origin credits Gutenberg with a system of steel punches, copper matrices and an adjustable hand mould, the method that let typefounders produce interchangeable sorts for the next four centuries. If the earliest Mainz types were instead cast from temporary or multiple matrices, the hand mould becomes a later development, possibly from the 1460s, and the chronology of technical invention, the roles of Gutenberg, Fust and Schoeffer, and comparisons with East Asian metal type all need revision. Methods for attributing and dating incunabula from type damage and sort identity also depend on what a 'single sort' is.
stuck: Agüera y Arcas and Needham's computational clustering of the DK type found far more distinct shapes per letter than a single-matrix system should produce, but their full data and methods were only partly published. Critics, above all Reske, argue that inking, paper, pressure, wear and photography generate apparent variation large enough to swamp the signal, so that algorithmic clustering of printed impressions cannot by itself identify matrices. No surviving type, punches or moulds from Gutenberg's shop exist, so the argument rests entirely on inferences from printed impressions.
solved: A published, reproducible dataset of every instance of selected letters across multiple copies of the DK-type prints and the 42-line Bible, with a casting model whose predicted distribution of within-letter variation matches the observed one significantly better than the alternatives, and which is consistent with impressions from experimentally cast type.
approach: Agents can segment and register every glyph instance from the high-resolution digitizations of several B42 copies and the surviving DK-type prints, separating variation that recurs at the same text position across copies (press or inking effects) from variation that recurs across positions (sort identity).

Competing casting processes (single matrix and hand mould, multiple matrices, temporary sand or clay matrices, composite punches) can then be simulated and their predicted variation compared with the observed clusters.

Decisive confirmation would require collaboration with typefounders and materials scientists to cast type by each candidate method, print with period materials, and pass the impressions through the same pipeline.

existing.title: A View of Early Typography up to about 1600
existing.venue: Oxford: Clarendon Press (Lyell Lectures 1968); reprinted London: Hyphen Press, 2002
existing.note: Standard account of early punchcutting and typefounding by a practising typographer, treating the punch, matrix and mould as the basis of type production from the start.

existing.title: Johann Gutenberg and the Catholicon Press
existing.venue: Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America 76 (4)
existing.note: Argued from paper stocks that the Mainz Catholicon was printed in three impressions from reusable two-line slugs, showing that early Mainz printing used methods other than standard type composition.

existing.title: Temporary Matrices and Elemental Punches in Gutenberg's DK Type
existing.venue: In Kristian Jensen, ed., Incunabula and Their Readers: Printing, Selling and Using Books in the Fifteenth Century (London: British Library)
existing.note: Written up from work with Paul Needham first presented at the Grolier Club in 2001: image clustering of the DK type in the Bulla Turcorum, the Scheide B42 and other pre-1465 prints found hundreds of variant forms per letter and proposed temporary matrices formed from elemental punches (link is the 2001 Princeton announcement).

existing.authors: Aureli Alabert and Luz M. Rangel
existing.title: Classifying the typefaces of the Gutenberg 42-line bible
existing.venue: International Journal on Document Analysis and Recognition 14 (4): 303–317
existing.note: Cluster analysis of letters on a B42 page found several clusters for 'i' and 'a', which the authors read as evidence for multiple matrices per letter.

existing.title: Hat Johannes Gutenberg das Gießinstrument erfunden? Mikroskopischer Typenvergleich an frühen Drucken
existing.venue: Gutenberg-Jahrbuch 90: 40–59; English translation, 'Did Johannes Gutenberg invent the hand mould?', JGU Mainz, 2021
existing.note: Main critique of the computational argument: microscopic comparison of DK-type prints and later incunabula concluded that printing effects make algorithmic comparison unreliable and that the observed variation fits a punch, matrix and hand mould system.

existing.title: Editio Princeps: A History of the Gutenberg Bible
existing.note: Comprehensive history and census of the 49 surviving copies and fragments of at least 14 others, the reference point for locating copies to compare.

existing.title: Statistical Analysis of the Gutenberg 42-line Bible Types: Special Focus on Letters with a Suspension Stroke
existing.venue: Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America 115 (2): 167–183
existing.note: Statistical measurement of letters with suspension strokes in the Keio B42 copy as evidence for how sorts and their matrices were made.

existing.title: Analysis of the Gutenberg 42-line Bible types aided by type-image recognition
existing.note: OCR-assisted measurement of about 120,000 letters on 46 pages of the Keio copy; found that stroke-to-letter distances differ between 40- and 42-line pages and suggested strokes and letters were punched separately.

existing.authors: Luz M. Rangel and Aureli Alabert
existing.title: Two corrections to recent censuses of the Gutenberg 42-line bible
existing.venue: Journal of the Printing Historical Society, new series 3: 101–113
existing.note: Corrects copy-level details in the Needham and White censuses, relevant to any multi-copy comparison of B42 type.

holdings.name: Keio copy of the 42-line Bible, volume 1

holdings.note: The sole surviving copy of the German edition, printed in the DK type, per Princeton's record of the Latin bull.

holdings.name: Mainz Fragment of the Weltgericht (Sibyllenbuch fragment)
holdings.note: Partial leaf found in 1892 in a binding at Mainz and printed in an early state of the DK type.
